sources.news_title: Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer after surgery
sources.text:
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery to remove part of his right lung at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday, 13 October. The Vatican confirmed that the 71-year-old pontiff had lung adenocarcinoma, a form of lung cancer, and said the operation was successful.
Surgeons removed the lower lobe of the pope's right lung during a procedure lasting approximately 90 minutes. Laboratory tests conducted during the operation confirmed cancer that doctors had suspected following earlier examinations.

The Vatican said the procedure went according to plan and that Leo regained consciousness normally before returning to his hospital room.
The operation followed the discovery of a lung nodule during a routine medical examination. The pope had disclosed the finding during his Sunday Angelus address in St Peter's Square, telling worshippers that doctors had identified the growth at an early stage.
He said medical specialists had recommended surgery and that he had agreed to undergo the procedure.
The operation was led by thoracic surgeon Stefano Margaritora, working alongside the pope's personal physician, Luigi Carbone.
According to the Vatican's medical bulletin, surgeons used a video-assisted technique to remove the affected section of the lung, aiming to eliminate the cancerous tissue.
The pope spent approximately three hours in the operating theatre, including preparation and recovery procedures.
The Vatican has not disclosed the tumour's size or whether the cancer has spread beyond the lung.
Stephen Liu, a lung cancer specialist at Georgetown University in Washington, told Reuters that determining the stage of the disease would be essential for assessing the pope's prognosis and possible further treatment.
He explained that surgery alone is often sufficient when doctors remove a small tumour before cancer reaches nearby lymph nodes.
Further examinations are being conducted to establish whether the disease has spread, a Vatican source told AFP.
Leo arrived at Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, where crowds gathered to greet him. He waved to those waiting outside before entering the building.
The Vatican expects him to remain in hospital for approximately one week. His public engagements have been cancelled until 20 October.
Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state, said he had spoken with Leo before the operation and described the pontiff as calm despite the diagnosis.
Leo became the first American-born pope in May 2025, following the death of Pope Francis. Born Robert Prevost in Chicago, he spent much of his religious career in Peru before assuming leadership of the Catholic Church.
He had no publicly known history of major respiratory illness before the discovery of the nodule.
The pope is scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November, although the Vatican has not confirmed whether the trip will proceed as planned.
His predecessor, Pope Francis, spent several weeks receiving treatment at Gemelli Hospital for respiratory illness before his death in April 2025.

Doctors said they removed the lower section of the pope's right lung.
The Vatican said Tuesday that Pope Leo XIV was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgery to remove a lung nodule.
The Holy See Press Office released a statement from Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora at Agostino Gemelli University Hospital in Rome, Italy.
'As he is admitted to the hospital, we accompany him with our prayers. ... We are also deeply grateful for his teaching, which urges us to place the dignity of every person at the center.'
"As planned, the Holy Father underwent thoracic surgery. To ensure a radical resection, the lower lobe of his right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," the doctors said.
"An intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the preoperative examinations. ... The operation was successful, and there were no complications," they added.
The operation lasted about 90 minutes, and the 71-year-old pope awoke normally afterward, the doctors said. He was returned to his 10th-floor hospital room.
Holy See Press Office Director Matteo Bruni said Monday that the pope was expected to stay in the hospital for a week.
"As he is admitted to the hospital, we accompany him with our prayers, mindful of the close bond between our university and the Agostino Gemelli University Hospital Foundation," said Catholic University of the Sacred Heart Rector Elena Beccalli to Vatican News.
"We are also deeply grateful for his teaching, which urges us to place the dignity of every person at the center and to build dialogue and peace," she added.
The removed tissue will be examined in the days after the operation, according to Vatican News.
Bishop John Dolan of the Diocese of Phoenix, Arizona, released a video asking for prayers for the pope.
"We ask that you pray for him, though, and entrust him to our blessed mother, to, of course, Jesus her son, and we ask also that St. Joseph, who is the patron saint of the church, will bless our holy father, that he will continue to serve the church worldwide," he said.
"He has been a true blessing, and we ask that the Lord will bless him as he journeys forth," Dolan added.

Pope Leo XIV is the first American pope in the history of the Catholic church and was selected by the conclave of cardinals in March 2025. Although he was born in Chicago, Illinois, he spent much of his time in Peru.

sources.news_title: Pope Leo has cancerous growth removed from lung
sources.text:
Pope Leo had a cancerous growth removed from his right lung in a 90-minute operation on Tuesday and "woke up normally" after the procedure, the Vatican said.
A Vatican source said further tests were being carried out to determine if the cancer had spread.
"To ensure the procedure was radical, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed," the Vatican said in a statement.
The operation "confirmed the diagnosis of a pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the pre-operative tests", it said.
The 71-year-old pope was in the operating room at Rome's Gemelli hospital for a total of three hours and the operation lasted half that time.
"The surgery was successful and there were no complications," the Vatican said, with a source adding that he had requested dinner after the procedure.
Leo had entered the hospital smiling and waving earlier on Tuesday hours before the surgery.
The Vatican has said it expects the recovery to take a week.
His audiences have been cancelled until October 20 and the operation raises questions about whether the pope will go on a lengthy visit to Latin America next month.
The surgery marks the 71-year-old Leo's first hospitalisation since he became head of the Catholic Church on May 8, 2025.
In a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers on Sunday, Leo told crowds in St Peter's Square that doctors had discovered a nodule "at a very early stage" during medical checks.
"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene," he said.
The Vatican has historically been very secretive about the health of popes, but began to be more transparent during the illness of Leo's predecessor Francis, an Argentine who freely discussed his ailments. (AFP)

sources.news_title: Pope Leo XIV has lung cancer and underwent successful surgery, Vatican says
sources.text:
Pope Leo XIV, 71, has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma and underwent successful surgery on Tuesday at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung, the Holy See said in a medical bulletin. The operation comes three weeks before the start of his tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, whose schedule has not been changed.
According to the bulletin, a histological examination carried out during the operation “confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected by the preoperative tests”. To “ensure a radical intervention”, surgeons removed the entire lower lobe using a video-assisted technique. The pontiff spent about three hours in the operating room, though the surgery itself lasted about 90 minutes. “The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the Vatican said. After waking normally and a brief period of observation, he returned to his room on the hospital’s 10th floor.
A Vatican source quoted by the AFP news agency said further tests were being carried out to determine whether there were signs the cancer had spread. The Vatican had said the Pope would remain in hospital for about a week, and his schedule has been cleared until October 20.
Leo XIV announced on Sunday, after the Angelus prayer, that a lung nodule had been detected “at a very early stage” and was “well localised”. The Archbishop of Tokyo, Cardinal Tarcisio Isao Kikuchi, who met him on Monday, said the Pope had decided to have surgery as soon as possible because he wants to keep his trip to South America, scheduled from November 6 to 17, with stops in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he served as a missionary and bishop.
“Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly wasn’t expecting anything like this,” said Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin, who highlighted the pontiff’s “serenity”. It is the first serious health problem publicly disclosed since the start of his papacy in May 2025.

sources.news_title: Chicago doctors explain Pope Leo XIV's cancer diagnosis as local Catholics offer prayers
sources.text:
CHICAGO (WLS) -- Pope Leo XIV is recovering after undergoing surgery and confirming lung cancer at Rome's Gemelli Hospital.
Doctors removed the lower lobe of the pope's right lung during a procedure that followed the recent discovery of a mass. The disease is believed to be in its early stages and is described as the most common form of lung cancer. The pope is expected to remain hospitalized for the next few days while under doctors' care.
The pope arrived at Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday, where hospital staff and patients greeted him as he entered the lobby ahead of the planned surgery. He smiled and acknowledged supporters before the procedure, which officially confirmed the cancer diagnosis.
Dr. Justin Karush, a thoracic surgeon with the Northwestern Medicine Canning Thoracic Institute, said it had appeared likely the mass was cancerous.
"It was highly suspicious based on what they had previously reported that this was going to be a cancer. Now we know that it is, and they removed the right lower lobe of his lung, which is a very standard operation after you find the diagnosis of a lung cancer," Karush said.
The pope spent about three hours in the operating room, with the surgery itself lasting about 90 minutes.
Karush said outcomes can be favorable when the disease is detected early.
"If we can find lung cancers truly at a at a stage one, the treatment is surgery and surgery alone. Patients don't require chemotherapy, radiation, or any other treatments typically for a Stage 1 lung cancer," he said.
As the pope recovers, Catholics in Chicago and abroad are offering prayers and support.
At Holy Name Cathedral on Chicago's Near North Side, dozens attended a midday Mass, where worshippers reflected on the pope's influence.
Deanna Ludwin, who attended the service, said she is praying for the pope's recovery.
"We want a complete recovery for him, and that we fully appreciate everything he's trying to do to bring people together, all humans together," Ludwin said.
In Rome, Father Burke Masters of St. Isaac Jogues in Hinsdale is leading a pilgrimage of 115 people across the Mediterranean. The group had planned to attend Pope Leo's Mass on Wednesday but will instead pray for his recovery.
"I hope that Pope Leo knows how much he's loved and cared for by not only us here in Chicagoland, but you know people from all over the world, and he's doing amazing work already as the church's shepherd. And I we just pray that he can continue to do that for a long time," Masters said.
Doctors are expected to conduct additional testing on the removed lung tissue and the pope's lymph nodes to determine whether the cancer has spread. Meanwhile, Pope Leo is resting in his hospital room and is expected to remain hospitalized for the next several days.

Pope Leo Has Part of Right Lung Removed as Doctors Confirm Lung Cancer
The 71-year-old pontiff is expected to spend about a week in hospital, with public audiences cancelled through 20 October
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung at Rome's Agostino Gemelli University Hospital on Tuesday, 13 October. A postoperative medical bulletin confirmed pulmonary adenocarcinoma, a type of lung cancer.
The Vatican said the operation was completed successfully and as planned, with no complications reported. The 71-year-old pontiff returned to his hospital room following the procedure. According to the medical bulletin, he spent about three hours in the operating room, including approximately 90 minutes undergoing surgery.
Surgeons Confirm Lung Adenocarcinoma
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung at Rome's Agostino Gemelli University Hospital on Tuesday, 13 October. A postoperative medical bulletin confirmed pulmonary adenocarcinoma, a type of lung cancer.
The Vatican said the operation was completed successfully and as planned, with no complications reported. The 71-year-old pontiff returned to his hospital room following the procedure. According to the medical bulletin, he spent about three hours in the operating room, including approximately 90 minutes undergoing surgery.
Surgeons Confirm Lung Adenocarcinoma
The lower lobe of Pope Leo's right lung was removed using a minimally invasive, video-assisted surgical technique. The procedure was led by Professor Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon, working with Dr Luigi Carbone, the Vatican's director of health and hygiene.
The postoperative medical bulletin said an examination of the tissue during surgery confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected from preoperative tests. The procedure was described as successful, with no complications reported.
The diagnosis confirms that the nodule was cancerous, but the extent of the disease has not been fully established publicly. Further assessment, including the results of tests on lymph nodes, will help determine whether the cancer has spread and whether additional treatment is necessary.
The successful removal of the affected lung lobe does not, by itself, establish a long-term prognosis. Although the nodule had previously been described as small and localised, its initial appearance should not be treated as a definitive assessment of the cancer's stage.
Pope Disclosed Nodule Before Surgery
Pope Leo disclosed the lung finding during his Angelus address on Sunday, 11 October. The Angelus is a regular midday prayer led by the Pope, traditionally before crowds gathered in St Peter's Square.
He said doctors had discovered a small lung nodule during medical examinations and recommended removing it. He described the finding as having been detected 'at a very early stage' and as 'well-contained'.
A lung nodule is a small area of abnormal tissue that can have several causes, including infection, inflammation or cancer. Most lung nodules are benign, meaning they are not cancerous. Their discovery alone does not establish a cancer diagnosis.
In Pope Leo's case, examination of the tissue removed during surgery confirmed malignancy. The postoperative findings therefore provided information that had not been established by the initial announcement of the nodule.
The Vatican had announced the planned procedure in advance, saying the operation would be carried out by Gemelli's thoracic surgery team under Margaritora's leadership. Pope Leo arrived at the hospital on Tuesday and greeted staff and well-wishers before entering the building.
Hospital Stay Expected to Last About a Week
The Vatican said Pope Leo was expected to remain in hospital for approximately a week following surgery. His public audiences have been cancelled through 20 October to allow time for recovery.
The admission is the first hospitalisation of his pontificate, which began with his election in May 2025. However, it is not his first known hospital stay. According to the Associated Press, Pope Leo was hospitalised for typhoid fever in Peru in 1985, when he was serving as a missionary.
Gemelli has longstanding links with the papacy and has treated several popes. Pope Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, spent an extended period at the hospital in 2025 while receiving treatment for pneumonia.
Pope Leo is expected to stay in a hospital room near the papal apartment, which is undergoing renovation, per a report by AP. The dedicated suite has traditionally been used by popes receiving treatment at Gemelli.
November Journey Depends on Recovery
Before the surgery, Pope Leo was scheduled to make an apostolic journey to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from 6 to 17 November. An apostolic journey is an official visit undertaken by the Pope in his role as head of the Catholic Church.
The planned itinerary involves extensive travel, and the Pope's recovery will be an important factor in determining whether the trip proceeds as scheduled. No cancellation should be inferred solely from the surgery or the current hospital stay.
Peru has particular significance in Pope Leo's life and ministry. Before becoming Pope, he served there as a missionary and later as bishop of Chiclayo. He was also hospitalised in Peru in 1985 after contracting typhoid fever.
The published itinerary remains the planned schedule, rather than confirmation that the Pope will be medically fit to travel in November. His immediate recovery and the results of further medical assessments will help determine the next steps, including whether additional treatment is required and whether the South American journey can proceed.

sources.text:
The Vatican confirmed that Pope Leo XIV has lung cancer after a successful surgery removed the lower lobe of his right lung.
The Vatican said in a medical bulletin that the tests confirmed a diagnosis of adenocarcinoma, adding that preoperative tests hinted at the presence of cancer that surgery confirmed, per CBS News. Pope Leo spent three hours in the operating room and the surgery lasted roughly 90 minutes before he was cleared.
“The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said. “To ensure a radical resection, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique. Intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from pre-operative tests.”
The Vatican did not disclose the cancer’s stage and whether it had spread.
“The Vatican tends to keep these things under wraps, so there’ll be a lot of reading between the lines to try and detect what is the state of the pope’s health,” Candida Moss, the Edward Cadbury professor of theology at the University of Birmingham in England, told CBS News.
“We should also expect that, inasmuch as is possible, Pope Leo is going to continue to work,” she added. “We have a long tradition of popes — not just Pope Francis, but also Pope John Paul II, who had Parkinson’s for 10 years — who continued to remain as active as they could, and as active in Catholic liturgies as they could, right up until the end of their tenures.”
According NBC News, medical staff prayed the rosary as the operation started. It was led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
“Let us join together in prayer, asking the Lord to sustain our bishop, Pope Leo, and to comfort all those who are hospitalized here,” said the vicar of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, at the start of the prayer.
Prayers and well-wishes poured in from all over the world in response to the news.

sources.text:
ROME (OSV News) — Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer following a 90-minute surgery on Oct. 13 during which surgeons removed the lower lobe of the pope’s right lung.
Dr. Stefano Margaritora, chief thoracic surgeon at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, led a medical team in the video-assisted technique operation. In a joint statement with Dr. Luigi Carbone released at just before 10 p.m., the doctors said that the “examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected by the preoperative tests.”
“The Holy Father was in the operating room for about 3 hours; the surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes,” the statement said. “After the surgery, the pope woke up as expected and, following a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the 10th floor.”
The pope underwent the surgery in the late afternoon after being admitted to Rome’s Gemelli Hospital at 1 p.m.
“The surgery was successful, completed on schedule and as planned, and the Holy Father has returned to his room,” the Holy See Press Office said in a statement issued shortly before 8 p.m.
Pope Leo was expected to remain for one week of recovery in Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, located atop Monte Mario, the highest hill in Rome. The Vatican has canceled all of the pope’s scheduled audiences through Oct. 20.
According to Vatican News, post-operation tests will be conducted on the removed tissue in the coming days. The Holy See was expected to provide an update on Pope Leo’s condition the morning of Oct. 14.
Following the operation, Pope Leo had dinner and spent the evening in the company of Vatican staff members, according to Matteo Bruni, director of the Holy See’s press office.
Rosary for Pope Leo during surgery
The hospital’s chapel was overflowing with people on Tuesday evening as Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome, led a rosary for the pope’s healing as people anxiously awaited the results of the pope’s operation.
Among those who came to pray was Sister Alphonsa Manikkathan from India’s state of Kerala and her fellow sisters from the Daughters of Divine Providence whose residence is located near the hospital.
“We pray for the pope every day, not only today,” Sister Alphonsa told OSV News. “Jesus said wherever two or more are gathered and pray for something, he will give. So for his fast recovery, we are praying.”
Father Miguel Silvestre Bengoa from Spain also joined in the rosary at the hospital. “If the pope is suffering, we also suffer with him,” he said. “But we want also to see him again in the Vatican.”
“It was so nice to be close to the pope in this same hospital,” the priest said. “We entrust the health of the pope to the hands of Our Lady.”
Asking for prayers
Pope Leo’s operation took place just days after he first revealed to the world that he needed surgery at the end of his Angelus address in St. Peter’s Square on Oct. 11.
Speaking from the window of the Apostolic Palace, the pope announced that doctors had discovered a nodule in his lung during a medical examination, adding that the growth was detected “at a very early stage” and it was “well-contained.”
“The doctors believe intervention is advisable, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to have it removed,” Pope Leo said.
Since the pope’s announcement, prayers and messages of support have poured in from around the globe from prime ministers, presidents, religious leaders and Catholic bishops.
Pope Leo’s second hospitalization
This was the second hospitalization in the 71-year-old pope’s life, according to a recently published biography. Shortly after his election, Pope Leo said that he had only been hospitalized once in his life before becoming pope when he caught typhoid fever after recently arriving as an Augustinian missionary in Peru in 1985.
“It’s the only time in my life I’ve been hospitalized,” Pope Leo is quoted as saying in the book, “Pope Leo XIV” by Elise Ann Allen, calling it “a very significant” moment in his life that helped him more sharply focus on his new ministry.
Pope Leo’s surgery occurred less than one month before he was scheduled to depart for South America for what would be the longest international trip of his pontificate Nov. 6 to 17, with stops in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. The Vatican has not yet announced any changes to the trip.
Courtney Mares is Vatican editor for OSV News. Follow her on X @catholicourtney.

Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery, Vatican says
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery on Tuesday to remove a nodular lesion from his right lung, the Vatican announced.
The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a news release following the surgery, describing the operation as "successful" and with "no complications." It said the diagnosis of lung cancer was confirmed during the surgery.
The pope was in the operating room for about three hours, the Vatican said, while the procedure itself lasted 90 minutes.
"To ensure a radical resection, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," the Vatican said in a statement. "Intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from pre-operative tests."
According to the Vatican, the pope "regained consciousness normally" following the procedure and was then taken back to his room on the 10th floor of Rome's Gemelli Hospital.
In its statement, the Vatican did not disclose what stage the cancer was in or whether the cancer may have spread. It also did not detail what further procedures or treatment the pope may have to undergo.
"The Vatican tends to keep these things under wraps, so there'll be a lot of reading between the lines to try and detect what is the state of the pope's health," Candida Moss, the Edward Cadbury professor of theology at the University of Birmingham in England, told CBS News.
Leo, who was born in Chicago, is known for living an active and healthy lifestyle, including swimming and playing tennis, all factors that likely worked in his favor going into the surgery. He has maintained a busy schedule since becoming pope a year and a half ago.
Leo entered Gemelli Hospital in Rome through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him, The Associated Press reported. According to the Vatican, the team that performed the surgery was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon.
The Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo's audiences through Oct. 20. There was no word on whether Leo would be able to keep his planned trip to South America next month.
The typical recommendation for a procedure of this kind is to avoid air travel for about three weeks, which would put the pope right up against the start of that trip, which is scheduled for Nov. 6.
Moss told CBS News that Vatican protocol calls for the pope's cardinals and aides to step in and take up many of his duties as needed.
"We should also expect that, inasmuch as is possible, Pope Leo is going to continue to work," Moss said. "We have a long tradition of popes — not just Pope Francis, but also Pope John Paul II, who had Parkinson's for 10 years — who continued to remain as active as they could, and as active in Catholic liturgies as they could, right up until the end of their tenures."
While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post that he and his wife were "united in prayer" for the pope.
"May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father," Rubio wrote.
The Vatican had announced on Sunday that Leo would undergo surgery after a nodular lesion was found in his lung. According to the American Thoracic Society, a lung nodule usually measures less than a half-inch in size and is discovered using a CT scan. Fewer than 5% turn out to be cancer, according to the thoracic society. If a nodule is determined to be cancerous, it is usually a sign of early-stage lung cancer.
"The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I've decided to have surgery to remove it," Leo said in remarks during his Sunday noon blessing. "Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers."
Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer in the United States, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America, and makes up about 40% of all diagnosed lung cancers.
It forms in glandular cells on the outer parts of the lung and is likely to be diagnosed earlier than other lung cancers because it spreads more slowly, the LCFA said. Symptoms can include fatigue, shortness of breath and upper back and chest pain. Treatments can include surgery, chemotherapy, immunotherapy and radiation.
One of Pope Leo's 2 brothers also battling cancer
Louis Prevost, Pope Leo's older brother who resides in Florida, was also diagnosed with multiple myeloma earlier this year, his wife, Deborah Prevost, told CBS News on Tuesday.
Multiple myeloma is a form of blood cancer, according to the Mayo Clinic. It forms in plasma cells, which are a type of white blood cell, and then builds up in the bone marrow.
Deborah Prevost did not share what stage her husband's cancer is in, but said he is currently in a clinical trial at a local hospital where he is being treated.
She said her husband was first diagnosed with multiple myeloma in 2017, but was able to maintain it at a "very low level" after undergoing treatment in 2019 that included stem cell treatment and a clinical trial. He "fell out of remission" three months ago, she disclosed.
Deborah Prevost could not comment on the specifics of Pope Leo's condition, but said her husband and his brother spoke last week before Louis Prevost went in for his clinical trial. Pope Leo also informed his brother of his own situation.
"He [Pope Leo] called to let us know what would be happening," Deborah Prevost told CBS News. "We keep praying, keeping spirits up for both of them."

By Christopher Lamb, Barbie Nadeau, Antonia Mortensen
(CNN) — Pope Leo XIV is recovering at a Rome hospital after a “successful” surgery to remove part of his right lung which was found to have a cancerous growth, according to a statement from the Vatican.
The Vatican announced Tuesday evening that the surgery had concluded “according to plan,” and that Leo “has returned to his room.”
“The Holy Father underwent thoracic surgery as scheduled,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora in a statement. “The lower lobe of the right lung was removed using video-assisted surgery.”
Further examination of the lobe revealed evidence of pulmonary adenocarcinoma, a common type of lung cancer, they said. The entire procedure lasted about 90 minutes.
The surgery took place Tuesday afternoon at the Agostino Gemelli University Policlinic hospital in northwest Rome, a private medical facility that has a long association with the Vatican. The hospital stay this week is the first of his pontificate.
The 71-year-old pontiff told the crowd gathered in St. Peter’s Square on Sunday that doctors had discovered a “nodule” on his lung, which he had been advised to have removed. Leo said on Sunday that the growth had been detected “at a very early stage” and was “well-contained.”
The hospital has a special suite of rooms for the pope on the 10th floor, which Pope John Paul II famously dubbed “Vatican three” during his frequent stays there – St. Peter’s being Vatican one and the papal residence Castel Gandolfo, Vatican two. Pope Francis also spent an extended period there early last year when he was treated for pneumonia.
The pontiff has cancelled all his public events until October 20.
“Surgeries to remove a nodule are usually minimally invasive with a low rate of complications,” Dr. Matthew Triplette, medical director of the Lung Cancer Screening Program and specialist in pulmonary and critical care medicine at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle, said earlier this week. He added that patients normally stay in hospital for a few days and then continue their recovery at home.
“These surgeries to remove the nodule are usually minimally invasive with a low rate of complications,” Triplette told CNN before the Pope’s diagnosis was confirmed. “If this is cancer, the outcomes are quite good, with a 5-year disease free survival of (more than) 80% for the earliest stages of non-small cell lung cancer.”
The Vatican will continue to function while the pope is in hospital although anything requiring his signature will need to be postponed. A spokesman said Sunday that the pope will need about a week to recover following the operation.
The Vatican has no specific rules on how the leadership of the Catholic Church is transferred should the pope be incapacitated. Even if he is unconscious and undergoing surgery, the pontiff retains full papal authority.
Both Pope Francis and Pope John Paul II issued laws and statements while they were being hospitalized. Day-to-day Vatican operations are already handled by a separate team.
Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin told Italian media on Tuesday that Catholic clergy are all praying for the pope’s good health.
“We were all struck by the serenity with which the Pope announced this procedure,” Parolin said. “We hope he can resolve this issue as soon as possible. We are confident, but naturally, we are supporting him with our prayers.”
Parolin explained that he saw Leo yesterday evening, and that the need for surgery came as a surprise.
“We spoke very calmly,” he said. “Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly didn’t expect something like this.”
“It is something that, thank God, was detected immediately,” Parolin continued. “And normally, when these things are caught in time, they can be resolved.”
The pope kept his normal busy schedule Monday, holding back-to-back meetings in the morning before participating in a gathering of bishops and church leaders in the Vatican.
News of the first American pope’s surgery has led to an outpouring of well-wishes across the world, including from those visiting Rome. “We’re just hoping that his procedure is going to go well,” said Paul Kavulich, who was visiting Rome on a pilgrimage with his daughter on Monday and is from the pope’s hometown of Chicago. “And he’s got God with him – no doubt about that.”
The Vatican press office said the growth on the pope’s lung was discovered during “routine tests.” Leo is not known to have any underlying health problems, and he likes to keep active by playing tennis and going swimming.

Recurrent chest infections

by Courtney Mares

ROME (OSV News) — Pope Leo XIV’s surgery to remove a lung nodule on Oct. 13 was completed successfully, the Vatican announced that night.
The pope underwent the surgery in the late afternoon after being admitted to Rome’s Gemelli Hospital at 1 p.m. Rome time. Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the hospital’s chief thoracic surgeon, led a medical team in the procedure.
“The surgery was successful, completed on schedule and as planned, and the Holy Father has returned to his room,” the Holy See Press Office said in a statement issued shortly before 8 p.m. Rome time.
Pope Leo is expected to remain for one week of recovery in Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, located atop Monte Mario, the highest hill in Rome. The Vatican has canceled all of the pope’s scheduled audiences through Oct. 20.
The hospital’s chapel was overflowing with people on Tuesday evening as Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome, led a rosary for the pope’s healing as people anxiously awaited the results of the pope’s operation.
Among those who came to pray was Sister Alphonsa Manikkathan from the Indian state of Kerala and her fellow sisters from the Daughters of Divine Providence whose residence is located near the hospital.
“We pray for the pope every day, not only today,” Sister Alphonsa told OSV News. “Jesus said wherever two or more are gathered and pray for something, he will give. So for his fast recovery, we are praying.”
Father Miguel Silvestre Bengoa from Spain also joined in the rosary at the hospital. “If the pope is suffering, we also suffer with him,” he said. “But we want also to see him again in the Vatican.”
“It was so nice to be close to the pope in this same hospital,” the priest said. “We entrust the health of the pope to the hands of Our Lady.”
Pope Leo’s operation took place just days after he first revealed to the world that he needed surgery at the end of his Angelus address in St. Peter’s Square on Oct. 11.
Speaking from the window of the Apostolic Palace, the pope announced that doctors had discovered a nodule in his lung during a medical examination, adding that the growth was detected “at a very early stage” and it was “well-contained.”
“The doctors believe intervention is advisable, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to have it removed,” Pope Leo said.
Since the pope’s announcement, prayers and messages of support have poured in from around the globe from prime ministers, presidents, religious leaders and Catholic bishops.
This was the second hospitalization in the 71-year-old pope’s life, according to a recently published biography. Shortly after his election, Pope Leo said that he had only been hospitalized once in his life before becoming pope when he caught typhoid fever after recently arriving as an Augustinian missionary in Peru in 1985.
“It’s the only time in my life I’ve been hospitalized,” Pope Leo is quoted as saying in the book, “Pope Leo XIV” by Elise Ann Allen, calling it “a very significant” moment in his life that helped him more sharply focus on his new ministry.
Pope Leo’s surgery occurred less than one month before he is scheduled to depart for South America for what would be the longest international trip of his pontificate Nov. 6 to 17, with stops in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. The Vatican has not announced any changes to the trip.
Cardinal Isao Kikuchi, archbishop of Tokyo, who met Pope Leo for a private audience the day before the surgery, wrote in a social media post that the pope had told him on Oct. 12 that he wanted to have the operation as soon as possible to give himself time to recover before the trip to Latin America.
“He assured me that this is a minor operation and he feels nothing wrong with his body, and he said he had decided to go for the operation as soon as possible not to change his plan of Latin America visit,” Cardinal Kikuchi said. “We have to keep Holy Father in our prayers.”
